title: SL2 is the universal multiplicative covering of PGL2
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. All groups are affine $F$-group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], with closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Let $S=\operatorname{SL}_{2,F}$ and $Q=\operatorname{PGL}_{2,F}$, and let $q:S\to Q$ be the scalar quotient homomorphism of [lem-sfb-projective-matrix-central-cover]. Then $S$ is semisimple, its scheme-theoretic centre is $\mu_2=\{tI_2:t^2=1\}$, and $q$ is its universal multiplicative covering of $Q$: for every smooth connected group $E$ and every faithfully flat homomorphism $p:E\to Q$ with finite central diagonalizable scheme-theoretic kernel, there is a unique homomorphism $u:S\to E$ with $p\circ u=q$. Here semisimple means smooth and connected with no nontrivial smooth connected solvable normal subgroup, solvable meaning that iterated commutator subgroup schemes become trivial. A finite diagonalizable group is $D_F(M)=\operatorname{Spec}F[M]$ for a finite abelian group $M$, with group algebra basis $e_m$, multiplication $e_me_n=e_{m+n}$, and comultiplication $e_m\mapsto e_m\otimes e_m$. Smoothness and connectedness are [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme]. This includes characteristic two and does not assert that $\mu_2$ is reduced.

source.place: Proposition 20.31, printed p.418; definition of universal covering in 18.7 and the lifting property in Proposition 18.8. The scalar centre is computed by commuting a matrix with the two unit transvections.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-projective-matrix-central-cover] with $r=2$. It gives that $S$ and $Q$ are smooth, connected, affine and of finite type, and that $q$ is faithfully flat with finite central kernel $\mu_2$. Its Hopf algebra $F[t]/(t^2-1)=F[\mathbf Z/2\mathbf Z]$ identifies this kernel with the diagonalizable group $D_F(\mathbf Z/2\mathbf Z)$. This is a scheme-theoretic assertion even in characteristic two.

source.place: Proposition 20.31, p.418; scalar quotient as in Example 5.49.

proof.text: Compute the centre on arbitrary commutative $F$-algebras $A$. Write $g\in S(A)$ with entries $g_{11}=a$, $g_{12}=b$, $g_{21}=c$, $g_{22}=d$, and let $E_{ij}$ denote the matrix with a single entry $1$ in position $(i,j)$. If $g$ is central, the equation $g(I_2+E_{12})=(I_2+E_{12})g$ gives $c=0$ and $a=d$, and $g(I_2+E_{21})=(I_2+E_{21})g$ gives $b=0$. Thus $g=aI_2$ and $a^2=1$. Conversely these scalars commute with every matrix after every algebra extension. The natural equality of subgroup functors is therefore $Z(S)=\mu_2$, including nilpotent-valued points.

source.place: The centre computation accompanying Proposition 20.31, p.418; direct matrix calculation.

proof.text: To verify reductivity without rank-one classification, let $U$ be a smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup of $S$. It is normal in $\operatorname{GL}_2$: for $g\in\operatorname{GL}_2(A)$ pass to the faithfully flat free algebra $B=A[t]/(t^2-\det g)$, in which $t$ is invertible. There $g=t(g/t)$ with $g/t\in S(B)$, so conjugation by $g$ preserves $U_B$. The equations defining the closed subgroup $U$ descend back to $A$ because $A\to B$ is injective, also after any further algebra extension. Apply [lem-sfb-general-linear-reductive] to $\operatorname{GL}_2$ to conclude $U=1$. Thus $S$ is reductive.

source.place: Example 19.19, p.401; elementary scalar factorization supplies normality in GL2.

proof.text: Let $N\subseteq S$ be any smooth connected solvable normal subgroup. The field $F$ is perfect, since it has no proper algebraic field extensions. By [lem-sfb-perfect-solvable-unipotent-torus], its smooth connected unipotent subgroup $N_u$ is normal in $S$, and $N/N_u$ is a torus. Step 3 gives $N_u=1$, so $N$ itself is a torus. Apply [lem-sfb-connected-action-torus-rigidity] to conjugation $S\times N\to N$: the action is trivial, hence $N\subseteq Z(S)=\mu_2$ by step 2. A torus $\mathbf G_m^r$ cannot be a closed subgroup of this finite scheme unless $r=0$: its Laurent coordinate ring would otherwise be infinite dimensional, whereas a quotient of $F[t]/(t^2-1)$ has dimension at most two. Thus $N=1$, proving semisimplicity.

source.place: Example 19.19, p.401; Corollary 12.37, p.244, and the solvable-group structure used in Corollary 17.62(b), pp.372--373.

proof.text: Write $X^*(J)=\operatorname{Hom}(J,\mathbf G_m)$. The algebraically closed field $F$ is infinite: a finite field would make $\prod_{c\in F}(T-c)-1$ a nonconstant polynomial with no root. Choose $a\ne0$ with $a^2\ne1$. By [lem-sfb-sl2-field-commutator-generation], $S(F)$ is its own commutator subgroup. Every character $\chi:S\to\mathbf G_m$ therefore has value $1$ at every $F$-point. The coordinate ring of $S$ is reduced by [sbc-lem-smooth-geometrically-reduced], since step 1 gives smoothness over $F$. Apply [lem-wf-affine-nullstellensatz-vanishing] to the regular function $\chi^*(t)-1$: it is zero. Consequently $X^*(S)=0$ as a group of scheme homomorphisms.

source.place: Proposition 20.24, p.416, with its field-size condition made explicit; Example 18.17, p.391.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-special-linear-picard-zero] with $k=F$ and $n=2$ to obtain $\operatorname{Pic}(S)=0$. Its affine scheme is precisely the determinant-one matrix scheme defining $S$; this uses the scheme Picard group of invertible modules, not a Picard functor of a proper curve.

source.place: Proposition 20.30, p.417; Example 18.20 and the opening sentence of Proposition 20.31 refer to this Picard route.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-connected-group-characters-torsion-free] to any smooth connected affine $F$-group $H$ of finite type: its character group $X^*(H)=\operatorname{Hom}(H,\mathbf G_m)$ is torsion-free, i.e. $\chi^n=1$ with $n\geq1$ forces $\chi=1$ as a morphism of group schemes. Its statement has no restriction on the characteristic, so it covers the case where $\operatorname{char}F$ divides $n$ and $\mu_n$ is not reduced.

source.place: The torsion-freeness assertion in the proof of Proposition 18.19, pp.391--392.

proof.text: Let $f:H\to S$ be an arbitrary multiplicative isogeny of smooth connected affine groups, and let $K=\ker f=D_F(M)$ with $M$ finite. The exact sequence of [lem-sfb-character-picard-isogeny-sequence] contains $0\to X^*(S)\to X^*(H)\to X^*(K)\to\operatorname{Pic}(S)$. Steps 5 and 6 therefore make restriction an isomorphism $X^*(H)\simeq X^*(K)$. By [lem-sfb-multiplicative-character-antiduality], $X^*(K)\simeq M$, a finite group. Step 7 makes $X^*(H)$ torsion-free, so both groups are zero and antiduality gives $K=1$. A faithfully flat homomorphism with trivial kernel is an isomorphism: faithfully flat local lifts exist, any two coincide because their ratio lies in the kernel, and the unique local lifts glue by the sheaf axiom. This proves multiplicative simple connectedness of $S$.

source.place: Proposition 18.19 and Example 18.20, pp.391--392; the alternative proof explicitly cited by Proposition 20.31, p.418.

proof.text: Given $p:E\to Q$ as in the statement, step 1 says that $q:S\to Q$ is a multiplicative isogeny, and step 8 says that $S$ is multiplicatively simply connected. Apply [lem-sfb-simply-connected-multiplicative-lifting] to these two isogenies. Its hypotheses on the field, smoothness, connectedness, affineness, finite type and the scheme-theoretic kernels are exactly those in force. It gives the required unique $u:S\to E$ with $p\circ u=q$. Together with steps 2 and 4 this proves every clause, with no reducedness assumption on $\mu_2$.

source.place: Definition 18.7 and Proposition 18.8, p.389; Proposition 20.31, p.418.

proof_origin.place: Proposition 20.31 via its explicitly cited Example 18.20 and Proposition 18.19; Propositions 20.24, 20.30 and 18.8. Semisimplicity follows Example 19.19, expanded through solvable-group structure and torus rigidity.
